As we wrap up, I want you to know—if the kitchen has ever felt intimidating, or if cooking seems like a mountain you’ll never climb, you’re definitely not alone.
Moving from dread to comfort is all about those small, imperfect steps. Each one is a quiet act of self-care.
This isn’t about becoming a chef overnight or forcing yourself to love cooking. It’s really about giving yourself permission to do what works for you, to take shortcuts, and to just let go of that lingering guilt.
Here are a few things to keep in mind as you move forward:
Cooking is a skill—not some magical talent. You get better with practice, not perfection.
Shortcuts and convenience foods? They’re tools, not signs that you’re failing or being lazy.
Flexible meal planning can actually make life a little easier, and you don’t have to stress or feel guilty about it.
Every meal you make at home—no matter how simple—is a win, all on its own.
And hey, it’s totally okay not to cook sometimes. Self-compassion is way more important than sticking to rigid routines.
So, here’s what this really means for you: your kitchen doesn’t have to be a battleground. It can become a place of small victories, comfort, and maybe even a bit of joy—if you let it.
Start right where you are, with whatever you have, and trust that every meal you make is enough.
The world is full of impossible standards, but your kitchen is yours. Give yourself permission to do things your way, to notice and celebrate those little wins, and to rest when you need it.
Over time, you’ll see that taking care of yourself through food—however you do it—can be one of the most powerful forms of self-care.
You don’t have to love cooking to reclaim your kitchen. You just have to start.
